en: Mahāmudrātilakatantra-nāma-mahāyoginītantrarājādhipati (The Sovereign King of the Mahāyoginī Tantras, titled *The Essence of the Great Seal*). Toh. no. 420. Translated by Śes rab gsaṅ ba, Kam Chos kyi ye śes, and Phyug mtshams Dgra bcom.
In the language of India: *Śrīmahāmudrātilakaṃ nāma mahāyoginītantrarājādhipati*.

In the language of Tibet: *Dpal phyag rgya chen po’i thig le zhes bya ba rnal ’byor ma chen mo’i rgyud kyi rgyal po’i mnga’ bdag* (The Glorious Great Seal Drop: Sovereign King of the Mahāyoginī Tantras). Homage to the glorious *Mahāmudrātilaka*.
The Śrīmahāmudrātilaka Tantra. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Hevajra!
O Blessed One, sun of the wisdom-ḍākinīs, awakener of the secret heart-lotus!
Seated upon the pericarp of the secret lotus, awakening the heart-lotus, listen to my words out of compassion.
O Blessed One, you who are the very wisdom of the ḍākinīs, you who open the secret lotus— the heart-essence—
residing within the secret lotus at the navel: listen to my petition!
The Heart Essence (*pad snying po*) = *guhyahṛtpadmabodhaka* (also in Gambhīravajra). [Kāruṇya is not translated].
In the *Hevajra* tantra consisting of five hundred thousand verses, which is an ocean of gnosis,
that reality (*tattva*) which has been taught is the sixfold yoga according to the *Yoginīmata*.
O Jñānasāgara Hevajra, the tantra consisting of five hundred thousand [stanzas].
That which you have taught as reality, the text of the six yogas of the Yoginīs— [you have taught] that very thing].
O Omniscient One, Supreme Lord, all of that has indeed been known by me.
Indeed, it is known by me; however,
there remains a doubt as to what has been established here according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
I, the hero, know that Supreme Lord, the Omniscient One; yet,
regarding what the ultimate reality is like, I have given rise to doubt,
O Hero.
The Supreme Primordial, the Sound, and the Mere Sound are emptiness.
"O Lord, where is that yoga consisting of six [elements], which is bliss and superior even to emptiness,
situated?"
The method of the syllables and the bindus, the mere method, and the supreme among the supreme;
these are known through the six yogas. Where is their abode?
There are many points of divergence!
1.5 Why does the vital breath arise, and where does it dissolve, O Wielder of the Vajra?
O Vajrin, what is the night of the vital breath (prāṇa), and what is the day? What is the twilight, and what would be its rising?
From where does life arise? Where is the Vajra-holder destroyed?
What indeed is the Vajra-night? And what is the direction that has arisen?
Why is setting [of the sun] reckoned in the *nāḍī*, and what else is there?
The *nāḍīs* are indeed the characteristic of time; this is for the purpose of the secret [teaching].
At what time will he set,
and how long will he remain as the supreme lord?
"What is the characteristic of time? And what does that time accomplish?"
O Lord, where did those two known as Ālikālī originate, and from what?
How many kinds of external rasa are there, and likewise of bliss?
What is that which is called *kāli*? From where does the Sovereign arise?
How many varieties of taste are taught? And likewise, what is joy?
O Lord of Jinas, at what kind of time do these joys arise?
What existed before?
What is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) called, and what is meant by "vajra"?
You have spoken of the arising of Vajreśvara at the time of joy;
how is the dharmadhātu explained, and how is the vajra taught?
What indeed is the secret of the word "I"? Why is it spoken of?
What is declared by the word "supreme"? Reveal its meaning—that which is delightful.
How is the word "self" spoken? What is meant by "secret"?
How is it explained as "supreme"? Please clarify the meaning of "joy."
How many kinds of *kula* are said to exist, as well as the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and so forth? Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Rudra, and their Lord, Sadāśiva.
Brahmā;
his lord, however, [is Śiva].
To briefly indicate the distinctions of the families: what are the aggregates and so forth, the sense bases?
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, who is eternally peaceful.
Where were they born, from what place, and of what nature, O Great Festival?
How many kinds of mudrās are there, and how are they considered great? From where do they arise, and where do they abide? How is that which is the greatest of the great?
Please explain some of the specific varieties of mudrās; what is the Great Mudrā (mahāmudrā) like?
How are the different types of worship described, and what are the flowers used therein?
What kind of supreme [offering] does the great *Sajīvāṅga* attain? What are the various types of offerings to the Protector, and what is the nature of the flowers therein?
"O Great Protector, what kind of sacrificial offering (*mchod sbyin*) should be requested?
*Gambhīravajra [says]: "Life-taking!"* (1.13)
O Blessed One, what is the nature of the maṇḍala called the Supreme Self? O God, in what kind of tantra is it taught, and who is said to be the goddess there?
What is the Blessed One like, [who resides within] the maṇḍala of the supreme reality?
"66b" Then, O Goddess, what is [the nature of] the goddess, and for what purpose was she spoken of?
How many are the divisions of the cremation grounds, and likewise of the trees?
O Lord of Jinas, tell us correctly and precisely their respective positions as they are logically established.
"Bhagavān, where is the charnel ground located? How are the trees there described?
O Lord of Victors, please explain those charnel grounds and the trees."
The internal fire-sacrifice (*ādhyātmika-homa*) and the direct sequence of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
The assembly of yoginīs and likewise their secret discourse—
O Lord of the Great Festival, tell us correctly the true nature of yourself.
The inner fire offering of the Protector, the ritual of the five nectars,
the assembly place of the yoginīs, and what the language there is like— O Great Protector, please explain my own essential nature.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to All Tantras," in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*. (Note: Gambhīravajra counts a total of 54 questions.)
The cause [of this].
This is the first chapter, titled "The Cause of All Tantras," from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*.
The Blessed One said:
The Blessed One said:
This question is extremely profound, the most essential of the essential,
supreme; it is the secret of all Buddhas, higher than the highest, supreme.
The vision is authentic, its depth difficult to fathom; it is the supreme essence of essences.
The great secret of all Buddhas, the most supreme among the supreme, the perfect excellence.
Then, O beautiful one, the animals here are indeed called *apradhāta* (the non-primary),
for they are the masters of that [state].
Apart from you, there is no one else who is a vessel for the ultimate truth.
Therefore, I shall proclaim the most secret reality; listen to that!
The great gods and so forth, as well as the noble ladies, are there among the animals.
That ultimate truth is yours alone; O fair-faced one, you are the vessel.
Listen to that which is the secret of secrets, most delightful; I shall explain it truly.
First of all, one should clearly perform the consecration of the disciple;
then he becomes a worthy vessel for the secret and other [higher] purposes.
When a disciple who possesses intelligence is first properly empowered, at that time he becomes a fit vessel for the yoga of the completion stage.
First, by conferring the empowerments upon the disciple just once,
at that time he certainly becomes a vessel for the explanation of the Great Secret.
Without consecration, there is no attainment of the fruit, just as there is no butter from churning water. May it be so.
Likewise, even one possessed of accomplishment might, out of pride, reveal this tantra here without having received initiation.
Without empowerment, there is no accomplishment; it is like pressing sand, which yields no oil.
Whoever, out of pride, explains the tantras and oral instructions to those who have not received empowerment—
Indeed, that teacher together with his disciple goes to a most terrible hell, having met with total ruin.
In hell,
he should indeed be entreated with effort for the sake of consecration by one who possesses wisdom.

[5–6] Even if a practitioner knows the meaning of the tantra, if they are deprived of authentic empowerment, they will go to a terrible great hell along with their master and disciples. Therefore, one should serve the authentic guru with the utmost devotion.
Immediately upon the death of the master and disciple, even if they have attained *siddhi*, they will go to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should request the meaning of empowerment from the guru;
[one who is] a knower of the reality of the received empowerment, wise, and compassionate.
Having obtained one who is exceedingly noble, steadfast, wise,
and vigilant—
Having received empowerment and knowing reality, the wise one whose nature is compassion [teaches] that which is profound, vast,
and stainless,
completely free from harm and injury.
One who is a hero of great and perfect waves, free from stinginess, and of noble nature;
one whose body is complete and fortunate, and who is devoid of envy for sense objects.

Whose mind is always delighted, being solely devoted to great passion; whose body is complete and adorned with the major and minor marks; who delights exclusively in great attachment; who has utterly abandoned envy for sense objects; and who is always joyful in heedfulness.
Possessing all the characteristics of one who is fortunate, completely free from the object of envy, with a mind always full of joy, he has a singular mind of great passion. (2.9)
If such a Lord, who has reached the further shore and is all-pervading, is to be served,
then a disciple should be purified with effort by a teacher of that same kind.
When one knows that vow, one should act toward such a guru.
In such a manner, the guru should examine the disciple with diligence,
just as gold is tested by heating and the like, and a gem by water and the like.
Just as one would examine a maiden for truthfulness, so should one examine a disciple.
Just as gold is tested by burning and other means, just as a gem is tested by experts,
and just as a maiden endowed with happiness [is tested], so should a disciple be examined.
Therefore, one should examine [the matter] from every perspective and through mutual scrutiny.
It must be performed otherwise; there would be fault, and accomplishments would be far away.
Therefore, with great diligence, one should examine each other individually;
otherwise, faults will arise and one will never attain spiritual accomplishment.
Just as poison, when purified by means of mantras and the like, becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*),
so too a disciple who is impure may become pure through sprinkling (*sekādi*) and other rites.
[The reading *bhavet* is supported by the corrected portion of the manuscript (*\ms\pcorr*), while *bhāvet* is the reading of the uncorrected portion (*\ms\acorr*).
This verse is cited with attribution in the *Guṇabharaṇī*, p. 88.]
Just as poison, when thoroughly purified by mantras,
becomes nectar, so too the body of a disciple becomes stainless through empowerment and the like.
Whoever should grant what is called the consecration, one should look upon him as Vajrasattva;
one should look upon the Guru like the Lord of Serpents; one should look upon the Śrī-guru like fire.
One who bestows empowerment should be viewed as Vajrasattva;
the guru should be viewed as the King of Nāgas; the glorious guru should be viewed like fire.
One should view the teacher as superior to [all others], and one should view him as equal to a wish-fulfilling gem.
Just as [one extracts] from the head of the lord of serpents through mantras and ritual applications, [so should one view the Guru, the Teacher, as superior;
one should view him as equal to the wish-fulfilling jewel].
Just as by means of ritual application and mantras, an incomparable jewel that destroys suffering and poverty is obtained from the crown of the king of serpents.
He who, being deluded, employs mantras without application [of the proper ritual] will experience suffering.

One finds the jewel of the immeasurables, which eliminates all poverty; through the supreme application of perverted [practices] and perverted mantras, one certainly causes the beloved to be consumed by fire.
The teacher certainly burns away his [the student's] fruit with the fire of his speech;
[this occurs] unless [the student acts] with proper method and the practice of training and so forth.
By means of such a ritual procedure, and through conduct such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth,
From that glorious face,
the jewel known as reality (tattva) is obtained in this very life.
Just as fire burns wood and reduces it to ashes in an instant,
so too a teacher, when properly pleased, shall burn away sin entirely.
Otherwise, if one lacks respect, the fire of his speech will consume one's etymological analysis; just as fire consumes wood, it reduces it to ashes in an instant.
If the glorious Guru is thus pleased, [even] sinful speech is [purified] in an instant. The Venerable Lady said:
The venerable lady.
"Blessed One, who is established as the preeminent authority regarding the consecrations in this tantra?"
In this tantra, what is the supreme empowerment of the Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
Through the division of the fourth sequence, the fruit is traditionally held to be threefold.
The primary consecration is the first, and the second is designated as the secondary; thus,
within the sequence of the four consecrations, three are taught by way of their results.

First, the master empowerment (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is one; second, the secret empowerment (*guhyābhiṣeka*) is supreme. [The third] is the consummated (*samāpanna*), which is the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*); and the fourth.
The third is that which has reached completion, while the fourth is the ultimate;
the primary is of eleven kinds, and the twelfth is characterized as secondary.

The primary [twelfth day] is [to be observed]; the secondary [twelfth day] is not. To act otherwise would result in fault; success in the distant future would be impossible. Just as one entering [the body] by means of mantras and so forth must be purified...

*Gambhīravajra’s list: 1. water (*udaka*), 2. crown (*mukuṭa*), 3. vajra, 4. bell (*ghaṇṭā*), 5. name (*nāma*), 6–8. three pledges (*trisamaya*), 9. vow (*vrata*), 10. prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), 11. consolation (*āśvāsa*). And his equivalences: 1 (11) = Vajradharakāya; 2 = Saṃbhogakāya; 3 = Dharmakāya; 4 = Mahāsukhakāya.*
Third is the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*); likewise, the fourth is as before.
There are eleven divisions for the master empowerment (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), and the secret empowerment (*guhyābhiṣeka*) is the twelfth, supreme.
The thirteenth is the attainment [of the state], and the fourteenth is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
with respect to each initiation (*seka*), there is a stage (*bhūmi*), and I am the lord of them all.
Even the Lord [is thus];
the stages (*bhūmi*) are external, while the joys (*ānanda*) are internal.
Wisdom and gnosis are the thirteenth; likewise, suchness is the fourteenth. For each empowerment there is a stage; these are the lords of the stages, the sovereigns.

Thus, its cause and root are threefold, and the fourth is called the fruit. O Goddess, the fruit free from the three is either the third or it may be self-arisen. *Kalaśa* = body (*kāya*), *guhya* = speech (*vāk*), *prajñājñāna* = mind (*citta*). The fruit is devoid of these three; O Goddess, it is either the third or it arises spontaneously.
It should be understood through the three causal channels; its fruit is the fourth.
Alternatively, it is devoid of the three fruits, or else it consists of the three natures;
and that [nature] should be known through the distinctions of bliss and so forth, in sequence within the wheels.
Through the distinction [of the embrace], there is the meeting and the kiss; this is the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) and joy (*ānanda*).
Touching: the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*) [i.e., the secret initiation];
sexual union: the wheel of mind (*cittacakra*), special joy (*viramānanda*) [i.e., the knowledge of wisdom initiation]; fainting: the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*), innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
On the third day of the bright fortnight, one should sprinkle the vessel for the sake of a son.
The distinctions of joy should be understood according to the sequence of the wheels.
On the third day of the waxing moon, the disciple of superior capacity should be empowered.
Her lotus-like face was adorned with petals that were her eyes; she was graced by the qualities of her limbs,
her beauty,
and her charm.
The *rūha* [in *virūḍha*] must be long for the *Upendravajrā* meter to function; thus, it is original.

Note the *tilde* sign above *maṇḍitā*, yet there is nothing to correct here except that *maṇḍitā* is one syllable too long for the *Upendravajrā*. "Indeed, from twelve years up to sixteen years, or otherwise up to twenty years, [is the period] until [the goal] is attained."
Twelve years; sixteen years;
twenty years in measure—here, *dvi* does not act as a heavy syllable (*gaṇa*), while *daśa* counts as one long syllable for the sake of the *Indravajrā* meter.
*Gambhīravajra: A twelve-year-old for the secret [empowerment], a sixteen-year-old for the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), and a twenty-year-old to be discarded altogether!
O handsome one with long eyes, adorned with beautiful form and the marks of youth!
Twelve, or sixteen, or even twenty years of age if not found;
she who is over twenty years old makes accomplishment distant.
Therefore, [a woman] more than twenty years of age— whether she be a daughter, a wife, a sister, or a niece—
is a different mudrā; she causes one's attainment of siddhi to be far removed.
One should offer a cow, or a daughter, or a wife to the guru;
having first offered them with devotion, they should subsequently be honored with wealth and other gifts.
Having bestowed hundreds of various garments and the most excellent qualities of diverse jewels.
Then, with various materials, one should worship the Guru with devotion;
with hundreds of various excellent offerings and supreme victory banners made of diverse jewels.
One should worship him profusely with priceless golden garlands and strings of pearls.
"O Lord, from this day forward, I am your slave; [accept] this secret worship."
One should offer countless strings of priceless pearls and gold.
From this day forward, I am your servant; I shall worship you, the greatest of the great, with the four offerings.
Out of joy, a teacher of such a kind is to be honored with one's whole being;
for he is myself in the form of a teacher, and should be worshipped with diligent effort.
By means of such a ritual procedure, one should strive to worship the guru.
The form of the guru is myself; by making offerings to myself, one attains the siddhis.
(2.31) Therefore, having honored the Blessed Lady with the mudrā, one should worship her for the sake of the great purpose. (2.32)
But that which arises from [its] practice, O fair-faced daughter, is to be cast down.
Then, having performed worship with the great mudrā for a moment, one should attend upon it;
whatever arises from that attendance should be placed into the mouth of the disciple.
By joining the ring finger and the thumb, one should distinguish it through union;
in union, one should insert [it] within and encircle [it].
Then knowledge arises, like the sexual pleasure of a young maiden.
Just as,
by joining the ends of a large [cloth], one should bring the enjoyments inside.
At that time, authentic gnosis arises; it is like the bliss of a maiden. Furthermore, through union, there is worship by means of what is equal to breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having placed the *prāṇāpāna-hūṃphaṭ* mantra upon the tip of the jewel, one should move the vajra.
Having equalized the vital breath and effort, one should perform the offering with great joy;
having arranged the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ* at the mouth of the jewel, it should be fixed upon the arrow.
At that moment, just as there were moments of bliss previously,
so too should they be described with a joyful mind from the pleasure in the mouth of the Vajra Maiden.
At that time, during the mudrā,
how does joy arise by its very nature in an instant?
Thus, it should be explained regarding the mudrās; this is the definition of bliss. Subsequently, having entrusted [the object] with the hand of the disciple, one should examine it in this way.
Afterwards, O Padmā, perform whatever task must be done for the disciple, as conceived by your own being.
Therefore, having placed [the object] into the hand of the disciple, one should speak these words:
"By means of my command, which is free from conceptualization, act exactly according to the purpose of the lotus."
Because the Mistress of the Dhātus herself resides within his very heart,
Buddhahood is never attained by any other means;
and she is subtle, of excellent form, and characterized by innate bliss.
In the center of the heart of the lotus dwells Vajradhātveśvarī.
Until that is attained, there is no awakening through any other means;
it is the form of natural bliss, to be perfectly worshipped even in its most subtle aspect.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the examination of the teacher and the disciple, initiation, and the sacrificial fee, in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Examination of the Master and the Disciple, the Offering of Honoraria, and the Empowerment," from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*.
Now I shall declare another secret, more supreme than the supreme.
Now I shall explain another supreme and most excellent [teaching].
Within the body consisting of the five aggregates,
one should perform the meditation on the six wheels alone.
Perhaps it is the meditation on the six wheels themselves!

Gambhīravajra: the wind-wheel at the navel, foot, or sexual organ; the fire-wheel outside the navel; the emanation wheel (nirmāṇacakra) at the navel; the dharma wheel (dharmacakra) at the heart; the enjoyment wheel (saṃbhogacakra) at the throat; and the great bliss wheel (mahāsukhacakra) at the head.
[End of verse] This chapter is a copy of chapter 38 of the Vajramālābhidhāna.
Now, the secret shall be explained: the supreme, the most excellent, the highest of the high;
the body whose nature is the five aggregates, the wheel of the six senses of the Well-Pleased One.
This is entirely different, as it is also attested in the commentary;
the commentary suggests *surateśvari* as the vocative.

And in those [mandalas] which are like the shape of a half-moon, one should perform the walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) within the sequence of emptiness— or perhaps within the wheel of wind (*vāyucakra*).
Just as the moon appears in water though it is not contained within the water, so too does the reflection appear.
The half-verse from the *Jalaśreṇī*: "jala[5\verso]śrepyardhāna" (38.3).
Even as a form half-filled with rain, it dwells within the wheel of wind;
neither half-full nor full, it is seen like the moon in water.
Mahāmāyā, the mother of the world, whose characteristic is to be the support of all things without exception.
The support of all things without exception.
Subtle, inconceivable, unborn, non-dual, and like the sky.
The Great Magical Emanation, Mother of Beings, whom he has attended for countless eons—
she is supreme, more supreme than the other supreme, subtle, unborn, non-dual, and inconceivable.
The number of seed-syllables of the wind-wheel is beyond the reach of even the wise.
That which is within the fire-wheel (*vahnicakra*) is called the void (*śūnya*); it is of the nature of the bindu.
And that [is] within / in the middle.
The wind-wheel, the mother who gives birth, is difficult even for the Buddhas to find.
Within the fire-wheel is the single bindu, devoid of syllables.
The self-existent one, consisting of all syllables, omnipresent, and all-pervading,
who brings about the increase of bliss and is devoid of vowels and consonants.
Everything is within; it is the letter *yaṃ*. It pervades everything, and bliss arises.
He increases bliss; he is devoid of the [major] marks and [minor] signs.
He is the sole cause of the entire triple world, the creator of creation.
The sole [lord] of the entire three worlds.
The sound that is beyond the unstruck (*anāhata*), devoid of all forms.
The three immeasurable realms are the cause and that which brings about birth;
their mode is adventitious, abiding as the locus, and free from all conceptual forms.
He saw the Grandfather Brahmā and the other gods, who were devoid of food and deprived of their gains.
Moving like the tongue of a serpent,
it is neither syllable nor lotus, and is devoid of the collection of elements.
The entity is like a snake’s tongue; it gives rise to the noble lineage.
It is not a letter, nor does it exist as an element; it is devoid of the crescent moon, the bindu, and the ornaments.
Innumerable, imperishable, and lotus-born, it is situated within the emanation of the navel.
Situated in the center of the wheel of Dharma is the stainless *nādamātra*.
Unborn, innumerable, and inexhaustible— this is the manner of the ultimate truth.
It is known as the state of the emanation wheel, the navel of equanimity.
The mere manner of the wheel of Dharma is like a stainless clairvoyant eye.
(3.9) It is partless, without support, without attributes, and without abode.
Free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*), without support (*nirāspada*), partless (*niṣkala*), beyond comparison, and devoid of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
One of the two terms *nirmalam* or *niṣkampam* must be incorrect;
perhaps both are? (cf. Vāmaśiva 38.10)
The stainless, uncontrived state is without location and without form;
it is unmoving, ineffable, and without the movement of breath.
If even this supreme knowledge is thus [attainable] by the lords of the gods, how could anything else be difficult to obtain?
But [it is] situated in the saṃbhoga-cakra, having the form of *parā* and being the supreme nectar.
Those who possess the mode of supreme primordial wisdom are not known even by the Lords of the Thirteen;
they abide in the wheel of supreme enjoyments, the supreme form of the most excellent nectar.
Having entered into another, it exists in every form; likewise,
through the nature of dependent origination, it is intoxication, like the essence of wine.
It exists at the ultimate limit of the supreme vehicle, just like the power of alcohol;
it is devoid of all self-nature and forms, and abides as the very essence of formlessness.
The primordial supreme [reality], which is established at the end among all ends.
Unperceivable, transcending all characteristics, and devoid of every defining mark.
In the wheel of supreme bliss, the other-excellent, all abide at the limit of limits;
it is without a viewer or an object of view, and is devoid of all inauspicious marks.
O Sovereign of the God of Love, it has been described as that which is ineffable, immutable, peaceful, and whose nature is self-experience,
situated in the center of the interior of the six wheels.
O Mistress of the Suratas, [you who are] the sixfold womb.
Inexpressible, inexhaustible, and peaceful, it is the aspect of experiencing one's own innate joy;
through the grace of the guru, one will obtain the well-pleased lord.
Such is the great gnosis, whose nature consists of the six consciousnesses;
it is explained as being ultimately present in the center of the six wheels.
And their yoga is proclaimed as the attainment of the downward and upward [movements]:
twelve and a half, six and a half, as well as eight and eight, and likewise eight.
Twelve and a half,
and likewise eight times eight.
The determination by means of numerical conjunction is twice eight and four times eight.

[That is to say, the number of petals or channels per wheel is as follows: the wind-wheel has six; the fire-wheel has three; the emanation-wheel has sixty-four (the consonants doubled); the dharma-wheel has eight; the enjoyment-wheel has sixteen (the vowels); and the great bliss-wheel has thirty-two (the vowels doubled).
Through the union of above and below, it exists in the form of a sealed union (*saṃpuṭa*).
Twelve, six and a half, and likewise sixty-four and eight;
two eights and four eights— this is the wheel, the lotus, and the poison.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Nature of the Six Consciousnesses," in the *Mahāmudrātilaka*.
[The verse concerning] Mahāmudrā.
This is the third chapter from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*, titled "The Characteristics of the Six Yogas and the Essential Nature of the Six Wheels."
Listen, O Goddess, to the great yoga of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), which bestows fruit.
Bestowing the fruit of greatness.
The seventy-two thousandfold [teachings], both external and internal, are stainless.
Listen, O Goddess of Great Fortune! The supreme arising of the channel-wheels consists of seventy-two thousand; this is the explanation of the families of the channels.

[Śrī Heruka, born from the family, should be known as the Mother of All].

She who is red, with the luster of a red lotus, radiant in her two feet, marked by a trident or a conch between her eyebrows; whose forehead is adorned with three lines or who is clearly marked with a *śakti*; whose eyes are red from birth, and likewise whose feet and hands are red;
she who constantly plays there like a child with pigeons, dogs, and puppies—she is renowned as the wife of a hero (*vīrabhāryā*).

She who always worships the mark known as the *canaka* (or *vañcaka*) in her house is, without doubt, a ḍākinī born of the glorious Vajra family—she who constantly plays with a mouse, likewise with dogs and domestic fowl, and in whose house the vajra-mark is always worshipped; she is born of the glorious Vajra family, a ḍākinī dear to the heroes. She who has the complexion of a fresh cloud, slightly resembling pale white, who wears a silk turban on her forehead and diligently maintains the wheel in her house...

She who always worships with the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth, sings, and dances, should be known as a *ḍākinī* born of the Vārāhī family, possessed of great power. One who resembles a cloud of pure blue, who always wears a skull-cup upon her head, and who turns this wheel in her home while constantly making offerings to it—she is a *ḍākinī* born of the Vajravārāhī family, intoxicated with power. She who has the luster of black collyrium, who is jagged-toothed and fierce-minded, who is always delighted by bathing, who is pure by nature, and who speaks little.
Having drawn a vajra upon the ground, one should worship it at midnight. She who is born from the family of Nairātmyā should be known as the manifest Vajraḍākinī.

She has the color of the blue sky, high and fierce teeth, and always delights in bathing. She does not speak much, draws a vajra in her home, and worships it when practicing at night. She is the glorious Vajraḍākinī, arising from the family of Vajravārāhī.
A woman with the luster of molten gold, possessing excessive body hair, whose limbs have the fragrance of jasmine and blue lotus, who is fortunate and truthful in speech;
having inscribed a visible thunderbolt upon her forehead and likewise in her house, she should worship it constantly, for she is indeed filled with great pride.
According to the Tibetan [tradition], she should belong to the Khaṇḍarohā lineage:

possessing a complexion like refined gold, with steady eyes and many body hairs; one whose vajra appears clearly upon her forehead or within her home; a royal consort who is eternally graceful; a most fortunate woman who speaks the truth, exudes the fragrance of mālikā flowers, and performs vajra worship in her home—such a ḍākinī born of the Khaṇḍarohā family is the Sovereign of Wisdom.

But that woman who is exceedingly dark, always fond of all kinds of meat, who has a thunderbolt mark on her forehead, and is constantly devoted to those [forbidden] actions; she who always delights in the cremation ground, fearless, pitiless, and emaciated—she is a ḍākinī born from the family of Śrī Heruka, a worthy vessel for worship in the home filled with liquor; of this there is no doubt.

One who is extremely fond of meat, whose eyes are like black ointment or the sky, who always delights in cruel deeds in a subtle three-pointed form, who constantly frequents charnel grounds, who is fearless, heartless, and ruthless—she who is honored in his house with offerings of liquor and the like is undoubtedly a ḍākinī born of the lineage of glorious Heruka.
She who has the luster of the color of a fresh cloud, and whose left fang is bared—having drawn a battle-axe upon the ground, one should always worship it in one’s own home.
She too should be known as a ḍākinī born of the glorious Heruka family, the bestower of accomplishments; she is undoubtedly a ḍākinī. [In Tibetan:

She who resembles the color of a fresh cloud, and whose left fang is bared—drawing a battle-axe there, one should always worship it in one's own home. She is undoubtedly a ḍākinī born from the family of glorious Heruka.
O beautiful one, I have here briefly explained the family, the signs, and the forms of all the ḍākinīs; for a detailed account, [one should consult] the *Jñānagarbha* and other works.
The arising of the colors, signs, and families of all the ḍākinīs has been explained here in summary; the extensive version is found in the *Jñānagarbha*.
[Oṃ. This is the fifteenth chapter from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*, titled "The Emergence of the Ḍākinīs’ Forms, Characteristics, and Families."
Listen to this maṇḍala where I am present before your eyes:
first, from the syllable *ha* comes the syllable *hūṃ*, and from the syllable *hūṃ* comes I myself.
Listen, O Sovereign Lord of Mandalas, who abides as the self that is not other; you whose form is the manifestation of *hūṃ* are yourself the very essence of *hūṃ*.
From the syllable *hūṃ* arises a form endowed with the primary and secondary marks,
mounted upon a solar disc, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
From the form of the syllable *hūṃ*, the Form [deity] emerges, endowed with the major and minor marks, seated upon a solar mandala, equal in brilliance to ten million suns;
he is in union with you, who resembles a blue lotus.
With four faces, eight arms, and three eyes, he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, possessing the form of a blue lotus. Through union with you, he abides with his right leg extended.
Holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, the moon and the sun, a bow and arrows,
and a sword and a skull-cup in his arms.
The khaṭvāṅga [staff] is filled with a vajra,
a bell,
the sun and moon, and a bow and arrow; as well as a skull-cup (kapāla) and a skull-bowl (khaṭwāṅga), both filled with great blood.
At the moment of churning the churning-stick, out of the power of compassion that had arisen,
those [qualities] such as *rasa* (flavor) and so forth emerged as soon as that [churning] had begun.
From the midst of that, Vajravetālī emerged with the first wave.
Having brought myself to the state of bliss, and having sported with great joy and delight, she then emanated from the first flavor as Vajravetālī.
Having emerged, Māraghātinī stands at the eastern gate;
she has four arms, resembles a cloud, and is intent on drawing her bow.
Bearing a makara on her right side, her form is one of wrath;
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff in her left hands, she is full of pride.
Dark blue in color, four-armed, with bow and arrow drawn at his sides, holding a makara in his right hand and a *kapāla* and *khaṭvāṅga* in his left hands; he resides at the eastern gate.
Through the union of *punar-manthāna*, a second [deity] constantly flashes forth;
emerging as a vajra-flame, she is stationed at the northern gate.
Red in color, holding a fish in her hand, and three-eyed; the others are as previously described.

Furthermore, through the application of the yoga of churning, from the second *rasa* (flavor), Vajraśṛṅkhalā emerges—naked, three-eyed, red in color, and holding a fish; she dwells at the northern gate.
Then, when the third [flavor] is attained, Vajraśṛṅkhalā issues forth.

Established in the north, she is red in color, holds a fish in her hand, and has three eyes; the others are as previously described. Furthermore, yellow in color and holding a monkey, she is situated at the western gate.
Furthermore, from the third flavor, Vajraśikhara emanated; she is yellow in color, holds a lion in her hand, and dwells at the western gate.
Furthermore, when the fourth [flavor] arises, Vajravarttalī emerges;
with similar hands and resembling a *kunda* flower, she stands at the southern gate.
Furthermore, from the fourth flavor, Vajramekhalā emerges; she is white in color, holds a garuḍa in her hand, and dwells at the southern gate.
When the fifth flavor is reached, Vajramekhalā emerges;
she stands at the corner, playing the flute and the drum, and has a double form.
By means of those five offerings, Vajraghantā is emanated; holding a clay drum and a lute in her hands, she is the second form in the southeast corner.
When Puṇaḥ is produced as the sixth, Vajrapiṅgalā emerges;
holding a lute and a hand-drum, she stands in the southern corner.
Alternatively, from the *Ṣaṣṭhajanmanirukti*: "The emanation of Vajra-aṅgulī, holding many cymbals and a great drum in her hands, dwells in the southwestern intermediate direction.
When the seventh [emanation] has correctly emerged, Vajrahāsikā stands in the south, sounding a mṛdaṅga drum and [wearing] a girdle.
She who is obtained through the seven limbs of perfection is Vajrabhāskarī; she emerges from the adamantine throat, holding a clay drum and a lute, and resides in the northwestern corner.
Furthermore, when the eighth [limb] is attained, Vajrabhāskarī emerges, holding a staff and a lute, playing them with joy.
Having flowed forth, she stands in the northern corner as Mālabhaṅgikā.

From the eighth [letter], through the attainment of gain, the emanation of Vajrasūrya holds a *tamūra* and a *karattha*, and by constantly grasping them with his two hands, he dwells in the northeastern intermediate direction after having emanated and conquered all Māras.
Furthermore, from the arousal of the embrace, when the first joy (*prathamānanda*) arises...

Emerging [from the heart], Vajrasuratā holds a vessel of nectar in her hand; bearing the supreme mudrā with its face turned downward, she is clearly manifest. The Garbha-mudrā stands in the eastern corner, intensely eager for amorous play.

Furthermore, from the churning and the method of churning, the first joy arises; from this, Vajrasāgara emerges, holding a vessel of nectar in her hand. Having emanated, she dwells in the eastern direction, at the corner of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya). With the mudrā of the bhaga upon her crown and her index finger at the location of the aperture of Brahmā, she stands established in the northern direction.

Known as black, yellow, and red, she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture. From the supreme joy (*paramānanda*), Vajrasarasvatī emerges; holding a vessel of blood in her hand, she dwells in the southwestern corner.
Alternatively, from the *Durgati-pariśodhana*: "The Vajra-Elephantess, who has not emerged [from the womb], holds a vessel of semen in her hand and dwells in the northwestern corner.
They are black, yellow, and red, and they sit with their left legs extended.
Furthermore: "From the union of supreme bliss (*surata*), that which is called the Innate (*sahaja*) arises."
Therefore, I was terrified by you because of that appearance of blue light.
Furthermore, from the method of authentic churning, the innate joy arises; that innate joy is a great passion, a fiercely blazing fire.
O fortunate one, in that state, I have gone to the ultimate reality.
However, O Sovereign Lady of Passion, the innate *suruṣī* has entered.
There, together with the *khyo*, I am completely transformed by my very nature. I do not become non-existent; I abide in my own natural state (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, this essential nature is not within the range of perception even for the Buddhas.
Conventionally, the sphere of the perfectly awakened ones exists nowhere at all;

its own nature cannot be expressed, and it is difficult to find even for all the Buddhas. If the perfectly awakened one were to find [it] as a conventional form, then every task would already be accomplished by that alone, and not by anything else.
Therefore, you have played with me properly for the sake of my training;
I pervade countless other world-systems, yet I sport with you conventionally for the purpose of arising.
Otherwise, there would be no mother of the Buddhas, and nothing at all could arise here.
Indeed, all this would surely become stationary;
for if I do not engage in play, no Buddhas would ever arise. There is no doubt that everything would become motionless.
However, while abiding in my own nature, I bestow the state of the imperceptible.

"Then, being devoid of intrinsic nature, I shall say nothing further. Having seen the Lord (Bhaṭṭāraka) entered into his own true nature (svarūpa), all the yoginīs, having conceived an extreme state of dispassion, regained their composure and exhorted him with these kinds of songs: [In the supreme state beyond intrinsic nature, for that reason I am silent. Then, seeing the Lord entered into his own true nature, all the yoginīs, having conceived an extreme state of dispassion, regained their composure and exhorted him with these kinds of songs.
Arise, O Lord of the Gods, Great Bliss, Vajrasūrya, Sovereign of the World!
Listen, O Nṛtivinḍa; tell us today by what means our purpose may be accomplished.
Having heard [this], the nature of the self is realized; it is prepared in the ocean of existence.
Alas! Therein, one does not die; O you who are intoxicated by the pride of being a hero, this is the innate nature.
Therefore, alas, why do you act contrary to that innate nature? It is of the nature of emptiness.
May the Lord of Vajra grant the knowledge of the causes of all things, which is purified by the meditation on the nature of the vajra, the seed-syllable, the wheel, and the gestures.

Arise, O Lord who delights in great bliss! May Vajrabhadra rejoice and may I be glad! O Lord, were it not for you, I would be like a corpse; Through the flavor of your compassion, cause me to be born! O Lord, it is not a void of annihilation; O Lord, it is not the nature of emptiness. Vajramuṣṭi, may you rejoice and may I be glad! Open wide the lotus and sport, sport! A-la-la-la, A-la-la! Ma-la-la-la, O Lord who delights in excellence! Vajrahastinī, may you rejoice and may I be glad! If it were not for what you yourself have spoken, The Buddhas would not appear.
Thus, having arisen from the two seed-syllables *Aṃ* and *Hūṃ*, I am together with you,
possessing the form of a wrathful deity with a wheel and adorned with the thirty-two marks.
From the body of primordial wisdom, OṂ and HŪṂ arise here; you and I arise together.
Together with the wheel, the supreme wrathful form possesses thirty-two limbs, standing in the midst of the eight charnel grounds within the palace of the Victorious One at the seat of bliss.
Having entered into union with you, I too am Jñānaḍākeśvara.

In a state of bliss, you and I, in the midst of the eight charnel grounds, for the sake of the human goal which is the cause of birth, [shall practice] the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*). Kṛṣṇavarṇa is exceedingly beautiful, with hair blazing and standing upright.
Endowed with sixteen arms, he has three eyes and sixteen faces.
Dark in color yet possessing great radiance, with hair blazing like fire,
having sixteen faces each with three eyes and endowed with sixteen arms.
He stands upon the four Māras, adorned with four feet; nevertheless, he possesses a form identical to mine, complete with ornaments.
Together with you, Lokeśvarī, and the Wisdom Ḍākinīs, I—
residing within the solar mandala at the center of the triangle— shine forth,
possessing one auspicious face and two arms, the latter occupied with a bow and other implements.
Others [place] one foot of both [feet] upon Bhairava;
the remainder [is performed] with the grace of the *tāṇḍava* dance through the application of the *ālīḍha* posture and others.
You too are equal in form to the letter GA;
above Bhairava together with his consort, in the center of a triangle is a sun seat, with feet raised in a dancing posture.
By means of the ritual of wisdom and method, [he holds] a vajra and a vajra-bell.
In his hands [he holds] the wheel-jewel, the trident, the hand-drum, and likewise the axe;
the skull-cup, the khaṭvāṅga staff, the moon and sun, and the mallet;
and in two arms, the bow and arrow, as well as the Buddha and the Dharma.
Wearing a garment of human skin, the subduer of the difficult-to-tame, the Unwavering One;
Bhīmā, Vīrā, Surābhakṣī, Bhairavī, Dūtikā, and Balā.
Aśvagrīvā, Aśvakarṇā, Gajanāsā, and Gajodarā; Bhīmā, Vīrā, Madirā, Bhairavī, Dūtī, and Śūnyā;
Aśvagrīvā, Aśvakarṇā, Gajanāsā, and Gajodarā.

Pāvakī, Jaladharā, Mṛgāṅgī, Cāruṇaprabhā, Śaṅkhakarṇā, Śaṅkhaśikhā, Śaṅkhanāsā, and Mahābalā— Me ma, Chu rgyun ma, Zla ba ma, Nyi ’od ma, Dkon mchog rna ba, Dkon mchog gtsug, Dkon mchog sna, and Stobs chen ma.
Śaṅkhinī, Śaṅkhamukhī, Śaṅkhapadmanī, and Mahābalā;
Gṛdhrā, Gṛdhrāsyā, Śyenā, Śyenākṣī, and Śyenagāminī;
Rohitā, Raktanayanā, Raktakeśā, and Mahānagā.
Gṛdhri, Gṛdhravaktrā, Khorpā, Hormi, Gamā, Hormgo, Raktākṣī, Raktakeśī, Ratnā, Kapotavarṇā, Kapilā, Kālī,
Śaśikā, Mṛgā— these have one face, three eyes, various colors, and four arms.
The red and black female foxes, the rabbit, the mountain, and the fresh grass—[these are] the Mothers.
She has four arms and various forms; she has three eyes and a terrifying face. In two hands she holds a bow and an arrow, and in the other two, a flaying knife and a vessel.
With disheveled hair and loose garments, adorned with the five mudrās,
they bear garlands of vajras upon their foreheads and are intent on accomplishing all aims.
His two hands hold a drawn bow and arrow; the others hold a sword and a skull-cup. A vajra garland adorns his forehead, and his limbs are decorated with the five mudrās.
Such is the Wheel of Death, surrounded by ḍākinīs.
Together with you, I shall properly [dwell] in this supreme pleasure-palace; such is my great wheel (cakra), my abode together with you.
Therein are the twenty pīṭhas and two hundred and four [sites].
Relying on those clouds in the form of ḍākinīs, they assemble.
That which consists of twenty-eight sites is remembered as the site of the assembly (gaṇacakra).
Holding a vajra, bell, jewel, wheel, sword, trident, arrow,
sun, moon, *dgra sta*, *dam ru*, bow, and mallet; with a *bhūti* ash-sack tossed upward and a *gshin rje* skin wrapped around his waist.
She has one face and two hands, and her color is the same as mine. Adorned with all ornaments, her two hands draw a bow and an arrow.
These are described as the channels (nāḍīs) by way of their purified forms, through the yoga of non-duality.
Whatever happiness exists in these two, that I [consider] from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Since everything consists of pleasure yet is accompanied by the latent impressions of ignorance,
liberation is revealed in such a way that ignorance is destroyed.

Then, as for the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*): the sequence of the arising of the channels is supreme; each goddess has a single peak. Through that bliss and you, by means of the secret attraction, the wind awakens and enters the mouth of fire.
That [fire] too, by means of the wood of the sense-faculties, shall manifest its own intrinsic nature.
By means of union and separation, the wind causes the fire to enter within; through that,
the fuel of the sense-faculties is ignited,
and thus Caṇḍālī blazes forth, radiant with the light of the rays of gnosis.
It correctly burns away that which has a basis, characterized by the five aggregates and so forth.
Then, by the power of the rays of gnosis, [the essence] from the wheel of great bliss flows as a liquid from all the channels in the ultimate sense.
Then, through this nourishment, one will quickly attain a perfect divine body;
thus, with a well-composed mind, one should practice by means of the yoga of repeated cultivation.

The form of the aggregate of conceptual thought burns the entire body. By the perfect blazing of that fire, the wheel of great bliss melts. Through this melting, the supreme nectar drips from all the channels. Furthermore, the body is restored and the divine body is attained. This should be practiced with one-pointedness through the yoga of the "pressing" (gomaspa).
Or else, when not employed [for other purposes], it is employed for the sake of vision.
Nor is it so at all times, when primacy is thus postulated.
Even without an external mudrā, there is the arising of bliss; it requires merely looking, yet not everything is like that.
For if conceptualization arises afterwards, accomplishment will not occur.
Just as a single object in the dark is not seen in the absence of a lamp.
Having seen the lamp and reached it, one should subsequently abandon the lamp;
for the purpose is served by that [vision], and not by the lamp at all times.

Subsequently, conceptual construction arises; therein, no siddhi will be attained. Just as objects within a vessel of darkness cannot be seen without a lamp, once they have been seen by means of the lamp, the lamp should be discarded thereafter. One should diligently protect the vessel, for there is no further need for the lamp to perform its function.
Therefore, by such a method, the nature of the channels (nāḍīs) should be correctly understood; indeed, the lamp of wisdom brings about the end of all conditioned existence (bhāva).
The characteristic of the lamp is here the channel; the channel is the characteristic of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Alternatively, the means (*upāya*) has been explained as that which reveals bliss and liberation;
or rather, knowledge (*jñāna*) is the revealer within the wind, belonging to the side of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
That bliss which is first attained through wisdom is the supreme consecration of the knowledge of wisdom, belonging to the side of the generation stage.

The method is taught as being with effort; bliss is remembered as primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). That which is the nature of the primordial wisdom of bliss is obtained from the Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*). Now, this is the empowerment of the Wisdom of Prajñā; it is the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
That very same primordial wisdom of great bliss is established within the mandala.
And great bliss is of two kinds: the conventional and the ultimate.
That very reality, the primordial wisdom of great bliss, perfectly abides within the maṇḍala.
Great bliss is twofold: the conventional and the ultimate. It should be known as the bestower of awakening through its divisions, beginning with *ānanda*.
Because the supreme bliss of all joys resides directly within.
Therefore, I shall explain their two sequences; listen with respect!
From joy and the other [feelings], the two types of bliss are to be known. Listen with faith as I explain their two authentic stages.
Light, vibration, attachment, and fainting—
these four should be known in their respective order as being auspicious and rooted in the causal principle.
From the very beginning, when both are seen together, passion arises through their union.
Therefore, bliss arises, conjoined with the various moments:

the union of appearance and touch, and the movement—this is the fourth. It should be understood through the sequence. According to the system of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), passion arises for both through the gaze of the consort (*prajñā*); at that time, bliss arises, conjoined with the various moments (*vicitrakṣaṇa*).
When there is a single, respectful contact characterized by the consort, [bliss arises].
Then, supreme bliss characterized by purity arises here. When there is contact with that through faith, at that time the stainless supreme joy will emerge.
Furthermore, from the union of the sense organs and constant attachment, happiness shall arise.
And that is the joy of cessation (viramānanda) here, when the fire has been kindled.
Furthermore,
when one joins with that [consort] through the union of the two organs,
at that time, the separation from bliss will clearly arise.
When the melting of both has been attained and they are stainless,
the perfect arising of the innate (*sahaja*) is thus described:
"When the fire of reality blazes from the two organs, at that time the innate joy (*sahajānanda*), which is beyond worldly existence, will arise."
The Bhaṭṭārikā said:
That which was indicated here for the sake of summarizing Ānanda and the others by means of the fourfold method—please explain that also in detail to me, O Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
The primary function of wisdom (*prajñā*), however, is the arising of bliss and the other [joyful states].
From the vision of wisdom comes desire; from desire, exhilaration arises for both. From contact, that very [wisdom] again, through the fullnesses, brings about the fullness of bliss.

When that very [bliss], through great passion, blazes forth, it is then that one experiences the supreme joy (*paramānanda*), which expands in an instant once that very reality has become certain. This initial desire experienced through touch is the first joy (*ānanda*). Subsequently, when that reality itself becomes fully manifest, at that moment it expands in an instant; this is the supreme joy.
Then the flame-drop, characterized by the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), radiates forth.
When that very [bliss] blazes intensely with the fire of passion, at that time the blazing drop is the descent of the joy of the separation of joys.
Both the Vajra-holder and the Lotus-holder take delight with reverence even in the bliss of cessation.
In this very way, the arising [of the object of knowledge] is likewise devoid of cognition.
The play of the vajra and lotus is the joy free from joy; that is the stage of generation (*utpatti-krama*), which is devoid of the wisdom of *u-ta*.
Furthermore, when there is forgetfulness regarding the objects of worldly existence...
When Utani goes alone in a single instant, at that time the *bindu* of Utani proceeds as the purification of the three;
then the deluded one recollects *Oṃ Ā*, the *bindu* whose nature is bliss.

Thus is the Blessed Lady Prajñā from the perspective of the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*). Then, there, she produces the coemergent bliss that is like a vajra; she is the Blessed Wisdom-Mother, the side of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
Wherein she spreads the coemergent joy in an instant, like a vajra.
In that regard, O Sovereign Lady of Delight, I am perfectly pervasive and none other; [the word] "ta" indicates bliss. Furthermore, I shall explain the fourfold yoga of this very [state] in brief.
The bliss of desire, trembling, melting, and likewise the state of bliss.
In this regard, I shall explain the four yogas in detail: desire, trembling, movement, and joy—these are the four.
This is the first yoga: attachment, the knowledge of its determination, full bliss, and likewise stability; from that arises the supreme.
That is the first application; that is the meaning of joy (*ānanda*). Expansion, eagerness, emergence, and supreme joy—these are the four joys.
Thus, in the west, the second yoga is the determination of supreme joy (*paramānanda*):
the joy of the flame, the drop, that called the whirlwind, and likewise the cessation (*virama*).
That is the second yoga; it is the meaning of supreme joy (*paramānanda*). Blazing, the drop (*bindu*), intoxication, and the absence of joy (*viramānanda*)—these are the four.
Thus is the third yoga, the determination of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*): *Oṃ*, joy, sound (*nāda*), the tranquil, and likewise the innate (*sahaja*).
That is the third yoga; it is the meaning of joy devoid of passion (*viramānanda*). Utterance (*uccāra*), method (*vidhi*), and sleep (*nidrā*) constitute the fourth, the innate joy (*sahajānanda*);
thus the fourth yoga has been explained. This tetrad, determined by the name "the Innate," shines forth indeed through the sixteenfold division of bliss.
That is the fourth application; there are sixteen distinctions of joy. These four are not other than this; here, the supreme meaning becomes as follows:
Therefore, by means of the sequence of the drops (*bindu*), its primary meaning is certain;
that which is produced from wisdom (*prajñā*) is known as the bliss of desire (*kāmānanda*).

Desire is explained as longing; it is stirred by the glorious Prajñā. Therefore, seeing that one's own mind is agitated, one should not let go of it, until the Blessed Lady Prajñā reaches fullness through great passion.
When that [state] is attained, he then sleeps, having reached the supreme beyond completion.
Therefore, when that fire, both external and internal, blazes for a long time through right application, then supreme bliss melts [the drops] from the crown of the head.
The pervasive flame becomes the emitted [state], characterized by the bliss of cessation (viramānanda).
Again, O Goddess, when her mind is intent upon the family of her own bliss, [the state of] emission occurs.
When that is perfectly accomplished, he performs the summoning (*ākṛṣṭi*);
by means of that, the fourth state, characterized by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), shines forth.

That is stirred by desire; it is produced by one’s own mind. By the word "desire" (kāma) is meant joy (*ānanda*); it is produced from seeing. That very [joy] is the Blessed Lady Prajñā; when she is expanded by great passion (*mahārāga*), at that time she becomes expanded. This is the second, supreme joy (*paramānanda*). At the time of expansion, when both the outer and inner are intensely ablaze, at that moment *yan lag ga ra pa* melts instantaneously. Now, the drop (*bindu*) of that blazing is clearly manifested by name. That is the joy free from joy (*viramānanda*); it is explained as the third. Furthermore, that very Mistress is the supreme form of exquisite bliss; at that time, the summoning of *utā* brings about liberation from existence (*bhava*). That is the fourth, the perfect supreme, the teaching on innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
And that [bindu], through the upward draws, remains primarily at the end;
by means of the distinctions such as bliss (ānanda) and so forth, it is indeed the innate (sahaja), and nothing else.
Because it is called the very nature of consciousness, it is present everywhere,
from the uṣṇīṣa of the wheel of great bliss down to the space between the eyebrows and the hollow of the navel.
To that extent is the eternal abode of the Bindu, whose nature is bliss;
and to that same extent is the abode of the Supreme, from the Bhrūcakra up to the Kaṇṭhacakra.
From the end of the throat up to the heart, that which is called the *virama* is situated;
by means of this very [process], the second stage is further described.
From the navel-cakra down to the end of the three folds [of the abdomen] is the abode of the bliss of the bindu, according to the perspective of the utpannakrama.

From the location of the three folds at the root of the secret place, according to the description of the section on the knots, supreme bliss (paramānanda) is to be known; and that of cessation (virama) is now being described.
From the location of the knot (granthi) comes the "jewel-mouth" (maṇimukha), known as the seat of the stage of cessation (virama);
and from this very place, together with the Supreme (parama), comes the heart of the Innate (sahaja).

That is the invocation of Ut; it is at the end of the three liberations of the bindu, in the place of the innate (*sahaja*). Through the distinctions of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth, the stages of the innate should be known. From the crown of great bliss (*mahāsukha-śikhā*) up to the center of the forehead wheel (*lalāṭa-cakra*), that much is the place of joy, characterized by the single bindu. From the forehead wheel to the throat wheel (*kaṇṭha-cakra*), that much is supreme joy (*paramānanda*). From the place of the throat to the heart wheel (*hṛdaya-cakra*), that much is the joy beyond joy (*viramānanda*). Then again, the sequence of places is explained in order: from the navel wheel (*nābhi-cakra*) down to the secret foot (*guhya-pāda*), that much is joy. At the knot of the secret foot, that much is supreme joy. From the place of the knot to the jewel fortress (*ratna-durga*), that much is the joy beyond joy. That which exists within the tip of the vajra-jewel is the innate, the ultimate reality.

Thus ends the fifteenth [chapter], the sixteenth section, titled "The Division of the Joy of the Arising Stage and so forth," within the twenty [chapters] on the Overview of the Maṇḍala in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*.
This is the sixteenth chapter from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*, titled "The Mandala, the Distinctions of Joy, the Characteristics of the Bindu, and the Stages of Generation and Completion."
The Bhaṭṭārikā said:
Oṃ. Blessed One,
Lord of the Knowledge-Ḍākinīs, I have a certain doubt regarding emptiness,
the nature of emptiness, and likewise the *nāda*, in their proper sequence.

Where does gnosis abide, and from where is it clearly known? O Blessed Lady, Ḍākinī, a slight doubt has arisen in me: from what source is gnosis—whether in the form of rain or of a drop—to be understood?
The Blessed One replied:
The Blessed One said:
"The *nāda* is situated in the place of the forehead; the *śūnya* is established in the throat.
*Śūnyatā* resides in the heart, and *jñāna* is situated at the site of the navel."

The *cūlī* resides at the location of the forehead; the *bindu* dwells at the location of the throat; *chara* is known to be at the location of the heart; and *jñāna* dwells at the location of the navel.

Where those who have attained the state beyond conceptualization (*avikalpa*) from conceptualization (*savikalpa*) abide—at that place, for them, there is knowledge in this world, provided they remain at the station of the navel.
From conceptualization comes non-conceptualization; wherever one arrives when traveling, that is their natural state, renowned as the place of the navel.
When wisdom reaches the deathless, that is always their abode;
the deathless is the true nature of the bodhicittas within emptiness and the other [perfections].

When one goes to the abode of nectar, at that time it is remembered as "gnosis" (*jñāna*). Nectar is renowned as the bodhicitta; there are four drops (*bindu*), beginning with the method (*upāya*) and so forth.
These are further elucidated through the distinctions of bliss (*ānanda*):
bliss resides in the place of the head, while the supreme self (*paramātman*) is in the middle of the eyebrows.
Its locations are four, and it proceeds through the distinctions of joy: the drop of joy (*ānandabindu*) is at the forehead; supreme mindfulness (*paramasmṛti*) is at the throat;
that which is called *virama* is at the heart; and the characteristic of the innate (*sahaja*) is in the two channels (*nāḍī*).
Joy-free (*virama*) is at the heart, and the co-emergent (*sahaja*) is at the navel.
In these and similar cases, the shape is triangular, indeed at its summit.
The triangle, shaped like a pericarp, is clearly the innate nature of the vajra;
within this triangle, it is remembered as the supreme abode of all the channels.
Below the navel is the place of the three folds; at its summit is a triangle.
This triangle, shaped like a pericarp, is clearly the natural vajra.
The triangle is remembered as the supreme abode of all the channels (nāḍīs).

Through the application of the conduct of the channels, joy and the other [blisses] are attained. Above the forehead is a lotus; above that is the *uṣṇīṣa*. That is the great secret gnosis, which even the Victors do not know. In the three locations below the navel, the feet of the Moving One are situated above them. The actual three are the shape of the navel below; therein the form of the vajra is clearly manifest. Abiding in the actual three, it is the supreme, perfect location of the channels.
Lalanā and rasanā, as well as the auspicious vyomavatī—
these are all one and the same avadhūtī, yet they are considered threefold by way of conventional appearance.

There are two, Rasanā and Lalanā; if that third is non-conceptual, it is one in its non-conceptuality, yet conventionally it becomes three. Just as a *viṭaṅkāphalinī* [plant] exists in the form of a conch-shell shape, so too the three channels, distinguished by body, speech, and mind, are situated within the lotus.
That is exclusively a continuous chain, like a coiled snake. By way of the divisions of body, speech, and mind, the channels become threefold.
The tip of the vajra is the mind-vajra; the surface of the three folds is the speech-vajra;
and the region of the navel is the body-vajra—such is the determination regarding the three vajras.

The Heart is called the Mind-Vajra, the Speech-Vajra is the throat-mandala, and the Body-Vajra is known to extend to the forehead; thus the three vajras are explained in detail according to their definitive meaning.

In the heart is the Vajra of Mind; in the throat is the Vajra of Speech; in the navel is the Vajra of Body—this I have clearly explained in detail. Between these two resides the *prāṇa*, and likewise the *apāna* is situated there.
Because it dwells in the heart, the *prāṇa* wind is known as such; and that which nourishes below the navel is called *apāna*.

In its center resides the life-force (*prāṇa*); likewise, there is the subsidiary life-force (*upaprāṇa*). From the heart-center arises the life-force wind (*prāṇavāyu*), and from below the navel arises the nourishing wind (*āpyāyakavāyu*). When the descending-nourishing wind becomes powerful, then that life-force wind instantly moves to the upper position.
If the *apāna* wind were to emerge from the soles of the feet, at that time the *prāṇa* wind would travel upward on its path.
It is certain that [the *apāna*] resides in the place of fire (*jathara*) and at the root of the navel;
furthermore, when the *prāṇa* wind moves slightly downward from the head.

The nourishing wind (āpyāyana-vāyu) certainly establishes its residence in the location of the navel. Furthermore, whenever the life-sustaining wind (prāṇa-vāyu) moves outward from the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa), the nourishing wind also follows to its own place;
thereafter, the life-sustaining wind remains constantly situated in the location of the navel.

At that time, that nourishing wind goes to its own abode; it is the life-sustaining wind (prāṇavāyu) which dwells in the location of the navel. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Chapter on the Method of the Wind of Emptiness and the Movement of the Channels, in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*.
This is the seventeenth chapter from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*, titled "The Manner and the Stages, the Bindu, the Abode of Gnosis, and the Universal Conduct of the Channels."

The Bhagavān said:
The Blessed One said:
"This most secret question is not asked by anyone very often.
Listen attentively; I shall explain it clearly so that you may understand it perfectly."
This is the perfectly secret inquiry; it is not known by anyone. Listen, for I shall explain it truly:
through the union of wisdom and means, bliss arises constantly.
Then, one should proceed by way of the *avadhūtī* to the supramundane state.
When there is great bliss through the union of wisdom and method, at that time the non-conceptual path— the bodhicitta—
arises. When the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) is not abandoned by the yogin,
then the lotuses below turn downward and those above turn upward.
If the life-wind (*prāṇa*) does not remain at the root of the navel for even a single moment, how could this lotus, which is turned downwards, turn upwards in an instant?
Therefore, one should lead the mind above the life-wind by means of its opposite;
when it subsequently becomes steady, stationed in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Then, O Nādha, it does not leak here, just as [water] does not escape from a vessel that is without cracks.
When the water remains undiminished, then happiness remains established;
through that stability comes innate bliss, and from that, the inexhaustible state of Buddhahood.
The yogi certainly attains [this] in an instant, provided he meditates in this way.

In the center of its navel, the mind becomes stable. At that time, it does not descend; just as water remains without leaking in an unbroken vessel, so too will the mind become steady. One should meditate upon that for a moment; there is no doubt that one will attain Buddhahood itself. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the procedure for the meditation on stabilizing the bodhicitta, in the *Śrī Mahāmudrātilaka*.

The Bhagavān said:
The Blessed One said:
