Henceforth, thirteen lines from the *Āmnāyamañjarī*: "Having stripped that mudrā— who is sixteen years of age, beautiful, and overflowing with the essence of bliss— naked, one should first worship her with the *samaya* and other [pledges]."

Listen, O Perfect One, as I explain the meaning of the wisdom of empowerment. Having made a mudrā—beautiful in form, sixteen years of age, and possessing *śilā* and camphor—naked, one should worship her with joyful hands.
Then, through the yoga of union (*sampuṭa*), one should desire her again and again;
one should perform churning with little force until the arising of semen occurs.

Through the union of the lotus and mouth, one should repeatedly engage in desire; one should move [the vital energy] gradually. Just as the nectar arises, one should intensely cultivate the heart of the lotus when it has dawned.
Therefore, O Sovereign of the Gods, it is called the Ācārya-abhiṣeka.

When [the disciple] has been sprinkled with water and has become the foremost of all, he should be placed within a lotus. This is the excellent empowerment of the Mistress of Perfect Joy (Sujyeṣṭhīśvarī); this is the supreme empowerment of the master.
I shall explain the supreme secret initiation; listen with reverence!
When bliss is perfectly established for even a single moment in the secret place, then it is called "secret"; otherwise, it would be merely worldly.
May it remain well-established for even a single moment;
otherwise— Furthermore:
"Listen with faith, for I shall explain this secret empowerment. Whenever the mind resides in the secret place, that is renowned as the 'secret'."
The secret is the semen in the nine-petaled lotus; it is the secret within the knot.
One should make it most stable in that place; until then, the bliss does not reside anywhere in the lotus of the sky.
And I shall now describe the empowerment of wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñānābhiṣeka), which is difficult to obtain everywhere:
wisdom is said to have the form of saṃsāra, while knowledge has the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
I shall explain the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), which is difficult to find in all the tantras. Wisdom is explained as *nirvāṇa*, and knowledge is remembered as *bhava*.
In some places, *bhava* is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and *nirvāṇa* is of the nature of cessation (*viramātmaka*).
That which is the jewel-casket of the Buddha is said to be equal [to all] or perhaps even superior in some respects.

That saṃsāra is supreme bliss; it is the recollection of nirvāṇa, free from passion. Or rather, that which is renowned as nirvāṇa is the Buddha, the vessel of the precious lotus. Existence (*bhava*) is the gnosis of the female organ (*yoṣidbhaga*); gnosis has the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
In some cases, existence is supreme bliss; in others, it is remembered as being identical with that [bliss].
Knowledge is known as the casket (*karaṇḍaka*), the supreme abode of all bliss;
wisdom (*prajñā*) is said to have the nature of semen (*śukra*), while knowledge is remembered as consisting of bliss.

% *Saukhya* % | The *bhaga* of the woman is the mudrā; it is remembered as "wisdom" (*prajñā*). It is renowned as the vessel of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), the locus of the supreme bliss of all. Semen is known as "wisdom"; it is remembered as the experience of the bliss of primordial wisdom.
Consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is the state of melting; otherwise, it is the state of primordial wisdom, which is bliss.
And its cessation is called reality, characterized by innate gnosis.

The fourth [empowerment] is called "dissolving into light. It is the wisdom that is beyond time. That is the fourth cessation; it is characterized by natural wisdom (*svabhāvajñāna*). Fire, strength, density, sound, the blue lotus, the breath-movement, and the mind.
The womb, the moon, the sun, the terrible, the supreme sound, taste, and lightning.

By means of these— Light, Power, Cloud, Manner, Breath, Utpala, Earth, Lid, Essence, Moon, Sun, Darkness, Supreme, Sound, Taste, and Lightning— the bindu-images are proclaimed within the four [syllables].
From the Snow-Mountain (Hima) and the Jewel (Ratna) up to the throat, there are eight half-bindus.
Now, sixteen [moments] should be known: the stainless bindu of bliss. From the aperture of Brahmā down to the throat, there are four bindus.
Together with the four joys, they are joined with the joy of cessation (viramānanda).
As previously stated, these two are remembered as extending from the heart-lotus up to the throat.
In the [tantras] called Parama, it is taught that when two rasas are joined, they are combined;
from the heart up to the jewel [the crown], as far as the throat, they are traditionally held to be four.
In those known as the Sahajas, they are said to be conjoined with the two Rasas;
from Ratnakaṇṭhā up to the mouth, there is likewise his tetrad.
As long as [it lasts],
it is taught that these sixteen digits of the moon, joined with the two *vaśā*s, are the drops of bliss (*ānandabindu*) associated with those known as the *virama*s.

In its location are the four joys, endowed with two flavors; from the throat to the heart, there are likewise four such [joys]. These are the four supreme joys, endowed with two flavors. From the location of the heart to the jewel-tuft, there are likewise four such [joys]. These are the four joys free from passion, endowed with two flavors. From the jewel-tuft to the upper location, there are likewise four such [joys]. These are the four innate joys, endowed with two flavors. The sixteen joys are the bindus; they are well-remembered as the phases of the moon.
Those forms, however, are to be known as the *ālirūpas* in the wheels (*cakras*) in due order;
yet, as they have been described, twelve suns are likewise remembered here.
With twelve half-forms, there are the bliss-givers (*ānandamadānanda*), as well as the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the flavors (*rasa*).
The digits of the moon and the sun are said to be absent from the faces of Brahmā;
they abide in supreme bliss in the form of twelve half-digits.
Likewise, the other three, known as *virama*, are likewise described as being within the formed [state].
The co-emergent gnosis is indeed devoid of these and others, such as the three and the six.

One should know *kāli* as the drop (*bindu*) through the sequence of the four wheels. It is devoid of the face of Brahmā; it is my own face, endowed with flavor (*rasa*). That which is twelvefold is known as the sun; it is renowned as the *kāli*-drop. Half of the twelve is the bliss-drop (*sukha-bindu*), remembered as joy (*ānanda*) and supreme joy (*paramānanda*). The three drops of joy and the joy beyond joy (*viramānanda*) are free from the three natures. Furthermore, they are the very self of all.
Now, that one who is the self of all has been described by me as being everywhere.
O Sovereign of the Gods of Love, that which is called the "One with a Single" (saika) is declared to be fourfold; joined with cause and fruit, it is established in succession across four locations.
The emanation body, the enjoyment body, and the great bliss body— this tetrad, arising primarily from the body, should be known in this sequence.
Regarding the number of thirty-two channels, sixteen are the *bindus*;
the remainder are known as the *ālīs*, and they flow from the root location.

I shall explain the meaning of the four; regarding the four abodes, there are four empowerments, which should be known as the noble Lady Sugatā. In brief, according to the sequence of cause and effect, there are four: the Nirmāṇakāya, Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, and the fourth, the Mahāsukhakāya. These are the four bodies (kāyas), which should be understood in the ultimate sense. Within the thirty-two and a half [channels], there are sixteen *ali*-bindus; the other, the *kāli*-bindus, always flow through the path.

Āli-jñāna is the mind (citta), and Kāli is known as the mental factors (caitasika). That which is indeed my singular bliss is, however, presented as threefold according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
Kali-jñāna becomes the mind; Kali-jñāna arises from the mind. It is the single Great Bliss, yet it appears as the duality of the conventional.
The moon is the form of wisdom (prajñā), while the sun is known as skillful means (upāya).
The moon is the cause, and it is also the fruit; because it is the cause, the moon is both cause and fruit.
Wisdom is the nature of the moon, while method is the nature of the sun. The moon is the cause *ali* and the fruit; *ali* is the cause and the moon is the fruit.
The sun is the cause and the fruit is *ali*; the cause is *kāli* and the fruit is the sun.
From the center of the sun arises the lunar orb, the form of semen, which is great bliss.
The sun moves as the cause, Kāli is the fruit; Kāli moves as the cause, the sun is the fruit. From the center of the sun, the moon arises; the form of the seminal essence (khu ba) is great bliss.
Āli is the bliss in the secret initiation, and Kāli is born from the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna).
That which exists between these two is the innate (sahaja); it should be understood as such.
And first, that of the Lord of Yogins is said to consist of embracing and so forth.

Ka is the secret empowerment of bliss; A is the wisdom-gnosis empowerment; and between those two is great bliss itself—thus is its nature recollected. Through the touching, embracing, and so forth, the master bestows the empowerment. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Arising of the Moon and Sun as Cause and Effect," in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*.

This is the nineteenth chapter from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*, titled "The Teaching on the Gnosis of Empowerment, the Cause and Effect of Ali-Kali, the Arising of the Moon, the Channels, the Bindus, and the Joys."
The Bhaṭṭārikā said:

\versvege \vers % 20.2 The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower; the person who is like a blue lotus flower; the person who is like a jasmine flower; and the person who is like a red lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by ill will, not burning with ill will, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, burning with ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. Yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by sensual lust, not burning with sensual lust, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by both sensual lust and ill will, burning with both sensual lust and ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust and ill will. Yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by ignorance, not burning with ignorance, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ignorance. This, monks, is called a person like a jasmine flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a red lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by ignorance, burning with ignorance, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ignorance. Yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by sensual lust, not burning with sensual lust, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This, monks, is called a person like a red lotus flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Teacher has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking only this much. Friends, let us go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we remember it. “Yes, friend,” the monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, adding: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain to us the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we remember it. “Ānanda, the person like a lotus flower is superior to the person like a blue lotus flower. The person like a jasmine flower is superior to the person like a lotus flower. The person like a red lotus flower is superior to the person like a jasmine flower. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the person like a lotus flower dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by ill will... whereas the person like a blue lotus flower dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will... yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by sensual lust... whereas the person like a jasmine flower dwells with his mind obsessed by both sensual lust and ill will... yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by ignorance... whereas the person like a red lotus flower dwells with his mind obsessed by ignorance... yet he dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by sensual lust. Therefore, Ānanda, the person like a red lotus flower is the most excellent among these four persons. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the words of the Blessed One.
O Blessed One, please always explain the conduct of the Lord of Yogins;

Remaining unknown for one month either at the edge of a village or within a forest,
he should thus recite the mantra aloud— a sound that accomplishes all desires and goals.
The means of accomplishment.

oṃ vajrānalārkāmṛtadhara khacitāmananādidharaṇīdhara śrīheruka svāhā.

"O Kuru,
[take] her who is sixteen years of age, auspicious, and overflowing with the essence of good fortune."
"Perform the supreme practice: with a girl sixteen years of age, possessing *sila* and *karpūra*,
who is dark as a blue lotus and adorned with ornaments of passion."
Her limbs possess the fragrance of fresh sandalwood; she is skilled in all ritual actions.
He has a complexion like that of a blue lotus, possesses the fragrance of sandalwood, is adorned with graceful ornaments, and is skilled in all activities.
While enjoying [her] of beautiful eyes in seclusion during a time of happiness,
at whatever moment he himself beholds the shimmering mass of rays—
At that very moment, one should cause one’s own body to wander in various forms;
having accomplished the purpose together with her in the secret form, one should then [wander] separately in manifold forms.
In one place attached to passion, and in another devoted to dispassion;
in one place his appearance was tranquil, and in another his mind was filled with great pride.
In some places he was devoted [to worldly pleasures], and in some places he was peaceful.
In one place seized by disease, and in another with a body pure with happiness;
in one place subsisting on alms, and in another possessing the majesty of a great king.

Some were engaged in sensual desire, while others had minds free from passion; some possessed peaceful forms, while others had minds full of pride; some were consumed by illness, while others had bodies in perfect health; some were begging for alms, while others were great kings victorious in battle.
In one place naked and withered, in another pure with a radiant body;
in one place eating little, in another devoted to great feasting;
in one place possessing a sense of shame, and in another entirely devoid of shame.
In some places he remains liberated, and in others he is intent on conversation; [in some places] he abides in silence.
In some places they are naked and stained;

in some places they are pure and clean-spoken. Some are accomplished with only a little, while others are accomplished through much. Some act with wonder, while others have shameless minds. Some remain mute, while others proclaim loud sounds.
In one place there is always excrement and urine, and in another, even milk;
in one place he is attached to evil, and in another, he is solely devoted to merit.
In one place the self weeps due to its merits; in another, it laughs with great joy;
in one place it engages in gambling, and in another, it dances.
Great joy, dancing.
In some places they eat great raw flesh;

in some places they drink milk. In some places they commit sins; in some places they perform great merit. In some places they weep; in some places they laugh with singular joy. In some places they frolic and play; in some places they dance alone.
In one place he was intoxicated with wine; in another, he possessed the demeanor of a great Brahmin;
in one place he was like a skull-bearer (Kāpālin); and in another, he was like the son of a Caṇḍāla.
Sometimes he wanders about giving expositions of the Dharma, and listens with a sense of devoted interest.
In one place there is a magician, and in another, one created by magic.

In some places he has the appearance of a leper; in some places the conduct of a Brahmin; in some places the conduct of one with a skull-bowl; in some places he acts as a fierce servant; in some places he teaches the Dharma; in some places he listens to the Dharma; in some places he practices illusion; in some places he is free from illusion; and in some places he speaks falsehoods. In some places he has the dress of a fool; in some places he is deformed and very haggard; in some places he has the dress of a courtesan; and in some places he has the manner of a great libertine.

In some places he appears overcome by greed, and in others free from greed; in some places his nature is that of a living being, and in others he is devoid of consciousness. In some places he displays the form of a child, in some places an old man of many years; in some places the form of a courtesan, and in some places one who enjoys supreme desire. In some places he is drawn by avarice, and in others his mind is free from avarice; in some places he has the very limbs of an animal, and in others he is without consciousness.
In some places he is expressed by speech, and in others he delights in the Self of all;
thus the lord of yogis, the wise one who has attained mastery, dwells within his own self.

"In some [places] he is inexpressible, and in others he displays a perfect physical form; thus the Lord of Yogins acts with complete autonomy. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, on the Conduct of the Lord of Yogins, in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*.

The Bhaṭṭārikā said:
O Blessed One, please sever my doubt regarding the enumeration of gnosis;
what are the syllables of the wheels previously described?
O Blessed One, Ocean of Wisdom, I have a doubt that has arisen within me: Regarding the six wheels previously mentioned, what are their seed-syllables?
By which mantra is the nectar (amṛta) obtained and how is it employed? O Protector, how do the heart-mantra and the others come to be in conjunction with you?
By which mantra is there the consumption and practice of the five nectars? How does that essence of yours and mine truly exist?
And for the sake of protecting living beings, what kind of *bali* offering should be made here?
The Blessed One said: "In order to protect sentient beings, what is the manner of the gaṇacakra in the midst of the assembly site?"
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Bhagavatī, to the seed-syllables of the wheels previously mentioned."
Namely, *klāṃ mlāṃ slāṃ plāṃ ṇlāṃ ślāṃ*; this is the placement of the seed-syllables within the pericarp of each wheel.
O Goddess with beautiful eyes, one should place the six seed-syllables of the six wheels—*kṣlīṃ mlūṃ plūṃ jrlūṃ rlūṃ hlūṃ*—one by one in the center.
*Khaṃ raṃ laṃ saṃ yaṃ śaṃ* is for the wind-wheel (*vāyucakra*). *Bliṃ klīṃ jrīṃ* is for the fire-wheel (*vahnicakra*), which is called the triangle.
*Khaṃ raṃ śaṃ baṃ saṃ naṃ baṃ ni*—these are the six seed-syllables of the wind wheel (*vāyu-cakra*). *Bliṃ kliṃ dzliṃ*—the wise should place these at the triangle of the fire wheel (*agni-cakra*).

In the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇa-cakra*), one should double the following consonants: *ka kha ga gha ṅa; ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; ta tha da dha na; pa pha ba bha ma; ya ra la va; śa ṣa sa ha*.
(Excluding *va*, there are exactly thirty-two.)

Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa; Tsa Tsha Dza DZha Ñya; Ta Tha Da Dha Na; Ta Tha Da Dha Na; Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma; Ya Ra La Wa; Śa Śha Sa. These seed-syllables, doubled, are to be placed upon the petals of the Emanation Wheel (nirmāṇacakra). [The syllables] *Oṃ*, *Trāṃ*, *Hrīṃ*, *Āṃ*, *Khāṃ*, *Lāṃ*, *Māṃ*, *Pāṃ*, *Tāṃ*—these eight are in the Dharma Wheel (*dharmacakra*).
TRĀṂ HRĪṂ ŪṂ KHAṂ | LĀṂ MĀṂ PĀṂ TĀṂ: these are the eight seed-syllables of the Dharma wheel (dharmacakra).
A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ <Ḷ Ḹ> E AI O AU AṂ AḤ: these syllables are [placed] in the enjoyment wheel (saṃbhogacakra) by way of the non-clockwise path.

A Ā, I Ī, U Ū, Ṛ Ṝ, Ḷ Ḹ, E AI, O AU, AṂ AḤ— these two sets of eight wheels of enjoyment are to be written in counter-clockwise order. Furthermore, having doubled these syllables which are the names of the vowels,
they become the seed-syllables of the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Thus ends the procedure for the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*).
On a level and pure patch of ground, well-smeared with sandalwood, saffron, incense, and various kinds of excellent flowers for the sake of perfect enlightenment;
First, one should worship the earth below with various offerings, cloths, and other articles.
One should smear the area of the ground with wine and so forth; the wise one should worship the ground with sandalwood, the finest saffron, various excellent flowers, and diverse offerings.

She too should cause the maiden to enter the mantra-chamber with a consecration.

A girl who captivates the mind, possessing a divine form, twenty years of age, and unwavering— wherever the King of Mantras resides, one should first introduce her there and serve her with well-composed concentration through the yoga of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

The first of the sense-faculties (the letter *va*), the fourth of *anta-stha* (the letter *ra*), the third of the second [group] (the letter *ja*), and that which is adorned below by fire (*e*).
Taking the first of the fourth [group] (the letter *ta*), it should be joined with the eleventh vowel (*ai*).
And the third of the second [group] (the letter *ja*) is conjoined with the thirteenth vowel (*au*).
The third letter of the first group, adorned below by the fire-syllable (RA); then the fourth of the aspirates (HA), joined below with the sun (RA). % [GRA] % [HR]

This, joined with the fourth vowel, brings all beings under control.

Endowed with the fourth vowel, it brings all sentient beings under one's control; alternatively, that very [syllable] should be written. Likewise, joined with the second of the fifth [group] and the seed-syllable at the beginning of the third, it is the essence of the heart.
First, taking Vairocana, and then the third of the *ūṣman* letters;

then, having taken the seed-syllable of fire, followed by the first of the fourth [group].

The shatterer of the supreme mudrā.
It thoroughly subdues the mudrās of others.

Gambhīravajra remains silent regarding whether this constitutes a separate mantra; however, it consists of the first of the sibilants (ūṣman) joined with the last of the semivowels (antaḥstha), namely [ŚVA].

And then, having taken the *bhāskara* (the sun-seed), it is joined with the third vowel. It is endowed with the first of the *ūṣman* letters and the fourth of the *anta-stha* letters; then, the seed-syllable of the sun is adorned by the third vowel.

The fourth of the sibilants (ṣ), joined with the sixth vowel (ū) and adorned with the digit and the bindu (ṃ)—that is HŪṂ. This very syllable, which shatters even the most powerful mantras, should be written again as the deluder of all wicked beings. (Ṃ). That same one is written thus once more: HŪṂ.
The fourth of the *ūṣman* letters, joined with the sixth vowel and adorned with the crescent moon and the bindu; or else, that very same [syllable] written out destroys the mantras of others.

joined with the end of the *ūṣman* letters and the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) by means of the excellent mantra.

Place the *bhaga-mudrā* upon the head; with this mudrā, offer the *bali*.
Treading upon [the enemy] and looking upward, while uttering the sound "ha ha," one should visualize oneself as Heruka, adorned with bone ornaments.
Even if a Daitya equal to Śakra stands before him, [he would not tremble].
No fear should be felt there, much less for anyone else. What [is to be done]? One must act.
Even if asuras resembling Śakra were to appear before one,
one should not fear them; what need is there to mention others?
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Rite of Offering," in the *Śrīmahāmudrātilaka*.
This is the twenty-second chapter from the *Śrī-mahāmudrā-tilaka*, titled "The Ritual of the Torma."
Now listen, O beautiful one, to another procedure for the *gaṇacakra*, which is secret and most secret; therein the *cakra* proceeds.
Listen, O goddess Locanā! This is the ritual of the gaṇacakra;
there, the wheel of supreme secret delight is thoroughly turned.
*Gambhīravajra also attests something like: "That which is the supreme secret, most delightful;
all [beings] are of one and the same time, entirely free from all conceptual constructions. (23.2)
Devoted to the guru, established in meditative absorption, and adorned with virtues such as renunciation— [all these] are entirely free [from faults].
All are of one single commitment; all are free from conceptual construction;
they have abandoned stinginess and pride; and they are devoid of attachment and aversion.
And one should cause those with pure views regarding the means to enter the *gaṇacakra*.
Otherwise, a fault would arise, or else the wheel would not be accomplished.
One who possesses devotion to the guru, is endowed with meditative concentration, is free from envy, and is single-minded—
such a person should be diligently admitted into the joyful gaṇacakra by the wise.
Otherwise, there are faults, and the wheel will not be accomplished.
Those who possess both wisdom and skillful means, who are exceedingly beautiful and highly discerning, [are truly wise].
One should avoid those who are twenty-five years old and those who remain beyond that age.
Wisdom equal to skillful means is praised in all cases, provided it is free from the twenty-five [faults].
First, one should visualize a captivating and beautiful mandala of flowers in all respects.
Each [practice] possesses its own means and wisdom; it is not fitting for any one of them to exist in isolation.
First, with a joyful and captivating mind, one should draw a mandala of flowers;
then,
with a well-composed mind, one should perform worship according to that very same ritual procedure.
Being well-composed,
one should indeed worship the Leader with one's whole being for the sake of accomplishment.
For the sake of accomplishment.
Then, one should properly perform various offerings with one-pointed concentration; one should worship the guru with all one's possessions and with faith.
Thereafter, one who cultivates the vision of equality should worship the Gaṇa;
as long as the Leader remains, so too does the Gaṇa.
One should also strive to make offerings to the assembly, while contemplating equanimity with the mind.
Just as the Guru holds the mudrā, so too does the assembly;
one should diligently bring [the consort] at midnight, as prescribed by the Śāstras and other authorities.
Having worshipped him, one should cause [the offerings] to be placed upon the seat of the Master-Ācārya.
One should kill [the victim] with a trident or a sword; at midnight, one should take [the heart]. Having performed worship with various offerings, one should prepare the seat for the Guru.
Just as I am, possessing the form of Heruka and endowed with Mahāmudrā.
In the same way, O Sovereign of the God of Love, the Vajrācārya is to be regarded [as such].
In the center is myself as Heruka, endowed with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā);
he is taught to be the Guru, and I am the Lady Sugataratnā.
In the *gaṇacakra*, one should avoid storytelling, dispute, and such speech; likewise,
the spitting of phlegm and so forth, laughter, and the stretching out of the feet and other limbs.
In the center of the *gaṇacakra*, one should not discard saliva and the like.
One should not engage in conversation, nor should one stretch out the legs and so forth;
one who rises repeatedly shall not partake in accomplishment.

One should communicate the matter to be done by means of gestures, signs, secret language, and so forth. (Note: *pūrṇena* is written very oddly; check again. One should perform the communication of the task through mudrās, signs, and codes of speech.
One should diligently apply oneself to the symbolic gestures (*mudrā*) and the secret language (*chommā*).
One should not perform dance or song in the circle of the *gaṇas* without permission;
nor should one place a single-piece vessel of excellent characteristics before the leader.
Standing before the hero,
[he holds] a single-pronged [vajra].
Without the oral authorization (*ājñā*), the assembly must never perform dances or songs. A single-piece vessel possessing the auspicious marks should be placed before the Guru.
In its absence, [the site] is divided into three sections and worshipped with various flowers and other offerings.
Being well-composed, one should offer that which is complete with the awakening of knowledge (*vidyā*). (*Vajramālābhidhāna*, chapter 62)
Alternatively, the third section should be filled with divine liquor; one should worship that vessel with various offerings and sacrifices.
A separate vessel for the Gaṇa, filled with flowers and other offerings,
should first be presented as a great bali, accompanied by various kinds of edible foods.
As for the placement of the vessels in the gaṇacakra, they are adorned with flower ornaments.
One should first prepare a great *bali* offering consisting of various kinds of food,
and such a drink as does not cause one's joy to perish.
Having prostrated again and again and having formed the mudrā, one should cause [the disciple] to drink; thus it does not perish.
One should drink as much as possible so that one does not become devoid of joy;
one should prostrate again and again, and having formed the mudrās, one should drink.
Then, having purified all the edible foods, one should distribute them among the assembly.
One should perform the kindling and awakening [of the food] in sequence with the syllables *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ*.

Then, having purified all food, one should eat it;
endowed with the white moon at the navel and the supreme Hayagrīva.
One should first perform the purification of the nectar through the yoga of the final and initial letters:
saffron, sandalwood, vīra, camphor, and likewise musk.
With *HŪṂ*, one should properly employ the white vajra; with *ĀḤ*, it is thoroughly realized.
Having consecrated it so that it blazes with the light of Oṃ Kīṃ,
one should partake of it; this, combined with the five nectars, should be distributed among the foods and other offerings.
Thereafter, having established them in sequence, one should conceptualize them as fourfold.
Upon the central petal of one’s own tongue, place a white Vajrasattva arisen from the syllable *hūṃ*.
By means of that wheel, one should thoroughly satisfy all things— the outer, the inner, and the self.
By means of the union of the ring finger and the thumb, one should [worship] the Hero and the Heroine in successive order.
One should always draw forth the hero from the center, even unto the tip of one's own tongue.
Through the differentiation of the four wheels, all wheels without exception are to be purified;
the Hero upon the tongue of the Hero is the Hero of Heroes in the center.
And having placed the hero upon the face as well, perform a captivating worship.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Teacher, established in the pledge (*samaya*). (Vajramālābhidhāna, chapter 62)
At the time of worship, one hero should be worshipped in the mouth of [another] hero.
In the center of the two lotus pericarp-seats, the seat of the heroes is prescribed. O Goddess,
if a hero does not know the determination of the meaning of the heroes,
his fruit from the *cakra* will never be accomplished.
In the center between the two navels is the abode of the supreme among all heroes.
If one does not know the meaning of the supreme among heroes— that which all those heroes [know]—
one will never attain the maṇḍala of the assembly.
In this manner, one should gradually perform whatever [practice] pertains to the external and internal;
by that, accomplishment will arise, as well as the vision of another ḍākinī.
Whatever external and internal activities there may be, they should be performed according to this sequence.
By acting in this way, one will attain the siddhis, and the ḍākinīs will assemble together.
Sometimes low-ranking ḍākinīs enter there for the purpose of watching.
In that regard, one should never engage in dispute with the wise.
If another yoginī should come for the purpose of examination,
the wise should never entertain any doubt regarding her at all.
One should offer no more than a greeting; by means of the mudrā, it shall be a welcome.
In that regard, whatever the teacher himself does or speaks, [that is authoritative].
One should not engage in ordinary conversation; rather, one should request food with a mudrā.
Whatever the Guru there has spoken or whatever he has performed—
alternatively, one should carry out all activities as the Karmavajrī.
Because he himself is Karmavajrī, the Vajrasattva, and not anyone else.
Alternatively, the Karma-vajra may perform all purposes;
just as Vajrasattva sports, so does the Karma-vajra.
Yoginīs come again and again in various forms;
one should not stumble there, but should act like a hero.
He who performs even that which is prohibited and forbidden incurs punishment for his transgression.
When the Yoginī appears again and again in various forms, [one should know: *Vajramālābhidhāna*, Chapter 62, etc. etc. When the Yoginī comes repeatedly in diverse forms, [one should recognize her].
For the time being, do not be afraid; act in the manner of a hero.
When you are occasionally restrained, you should thoroughly understand that as punishment.
Then, when bliss has arisen, one who has attained realization should perform a dance;
and that he should do with vajra steps until the deities are satisfied.
When true joy has arisen, one should dance for the sake of liberation. Nevertheless, by means of the vajra-foot dance, how may the yoginīs be pleased?
Indeed, a mother, a sister, or a daughter requests that worship be performed.
By means of the ritual application of wisdom and skillful means, one should offer [it] without conceptualization.
With effort,
one should worship the mother, the sister, the wife, the maternal aunt, and the daughter-in-law,
according to the ritual of wisdom and method.
Through the worship of these, success is obtained; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having taken the offered oblation, one should follow while playing great musical instruments.
Through worshipping them, whatever siddhi one has conceived in the mind [shall be attained].
Having taken the remaining *bali* offering, one should send it away to a great wilderness.
If, moreover, the *yoginīs* should appear there once again, [one should act accordingly].
In this regard,
however, such a characteristic of these [women] must first be understood by the wise.
If one who possesses the characteristics of a yoginī is shown by the wise, that is the teaching.
These characteristics are as follows; they should be understood with effort by the wise. (23.31) One whose face has a reddish luster, is round, and is provided with a beard—
Whose facial disc appears perfectly round, whose mouth is always red like the *bimba* fruit, and whose eyebrows are long and excessively hairy;
Clad in white garments, gentle, unshakeable, and truthful in speech;
she who is remembered as a wife of heroes, reciting the true Dharma.
Remember that hero’s sister, who was pure, clean, and refined; who was steadfast and spoke the truth; and who always delighted in the sublime Dharma.
The lotus mudrā and likewise the tortoise mudrā should be given to him;
the deer skin and the water-pot are designated as the counter-mudrās.
One should bestow the lotus mudrā; likewise, there is the tortoise mudrā. The skin, the flask, and the ritual water-pot are to be known as the responses to the mudrās.
On the tenth day, his lotus should be drawn in the house.
At that tenth watch,
she who had long lips and large eyes became his protector when [he] was born.
On the tenth day of each lunar fortnight, she will draw lotuses in her home.
These very characteristics of the Guru’s consort are as follows:
her lower lip hangs down, her eyes are long, and they are red with a yellowish-white hue.

wealthy, fortunate, and endowed with virtues, she appears golden-hued like a *campaka* flower. She is neither very tall nor short, and she always takes pleasure in diverse clothes.

enjoys himself, and stands having traversed the path.

having seen such a *ḍākinī*, one should display the *śūla* mudrā.
Those who have died in battle always delight in stories [of their deeds]. Upon seeing such a person who is intensely proud, one should display the trident mudrā;
contracting the left leg, one should likewise perform a dance.

Having drawn a wheel in the house with sandalwood paste and other substances, one should worship it;
furthermore, two pits are always to be seen at the edge of Gaṇḍā’s [image].

Having drawn a trident in the house, one should worship it constantly; these are the characteristics of the Guru, the Lord of the World (Lokanātha). Wherever the mother’s womb appears as a dark cavity, [there he dwells].
Reddish-white in complexion, with red hands and eyes of extreme compassion,
her hair is likewise curled, and she wears a silk turban upon her head.

Likewise, [his] hands were reddish-yellow, his eyes appeared greenish-yellow, his hair was curled, and a silk cloth was bound upon his head. His forehead was shaped like a bow, and his face was like the upward-facing crescent moon.

With a long neck and a long nose, she always delights in red garments. She clearly resides in the form of a bow upon the forehead; likewise, she has a long neck and a long nose, and always takes pleasure in red clothing.
She laughs and plays constantly, yet she becomes angry without cause;
with a particularly fickle mind, she seeks out quarrels in an instant.
Sometimes they dance and sing, sometimes they become angry; their minds are restless, and they delight in quarreling.
Having seen such a mother, one should cause the Śakti-mudrā to be given;
the Ghaṇṭā-mudrā should also be diligently offered as the second, for she is indeed that very same one.
Having seen one who is so excessively arrogant, one should display the śakti-mudrā; with the second [hand], one should diligently display the ghaṇṭā-mudrā.
Furthermore, the counter-mudrā (pratimudrā) is performed with the left [hand].
The fourteenth and the eighth days are indeed prescribed as his festivals.
Turning toward the left side is taught to be the response to the mudrā.
And one should worship a wheel drawn in the house with white and blue lotuses.
She is short, thick-waisted, dark-complexioned, thick-thighed, and renowned.
Short and with thick calves;
Always fond of yellow garments and with her cloth draped over her shoulder—
one who sees such a female wanderer on earth should cause the wheel-seal (cakramudrā) to be bestowed.
Upon seeing a woman who always delights in yellow garments and whose clothes hang down from her shoulders, one should perform the wheel mudrā;
furthermore,
one should diligently apply the second, the conch mudrā.

On the new moon day and on the fourteenth day— the festival prescribed for those days—
one should always write [this] in one's home and worship it with *madana* and other offerings.
The fourteenth day is the time for that; one should draw a vajra in his house. These are the characteristics of the glorious Heruka as the Guru.
Her entire body was covered in hair, her eyes were black and tawny,
she was formidable, deformed, and terrible; she had a thick face and thick shoulders.
Her entire body was covered in hair; her eyes were dark and yellow; she was thick-set and of hideous appearance; her face was swollen and large;
she had sunken eyes, protruding lips, a broken nose, and a radiance like that of a corpse.

Skilled in dance and music, always delighting in the drinking of intoxicants, with protruding lips and a dark complexion, round eyes and a deformed nose, constantly expert in song and dance, cloud-like in form and large-bellied.
Having seen such a ḍākinī, one should cause the *napā* mudrā to be presented; furthermore,
the *śakti* mudrā should be diligently presented as the second.
Seeing such extreme arrogance, one should display the mudrā of song; furthermore, with diligence, one should display the second, the mudrā of the spear.

on the eleventh and twelfth [days], one should consume the *acala* together with *bhokṣa*.
If [the gesture] is turned completely to the left, it is explained as being the response-mudrā. On the eleventh day of that month,
one should always draw a fang in the house and worship it with saffron and other substances.

These should be recognized with effort by the wise on the path at night; these are the characteristics of Vajravārāhī, who appears as a house-demoness. Thus, one should strive to know her during the time of night.
They should not fear anything; one should always worship them with mudrās and other offerings.
When satisfied, they grant whatever accomplishment resides in one's mind.
One should not fear any of them; one should please them with mudrās. Once pleased, they will grant accomplishments exactly as one has envisioned.

by the mere consumption of which accomplishment quickly proceeds.

With very supple limbs, fragrant body, and adorned with sweet-smelling sweat,
truthful and possessed of a modest nature, he always dwells for a long time [in that state].

by merely consuming it, one becomes possessed of knowledge of the three worlds.

The Blessed One said:

in the space of the pericarp of both, which is free from the unevenness of the needle-point.

Wisdom, known by the form of Caṇḍālī, bestows bliss even though she is formless; though her touch is that of an ascetic, her touch is wondrous, and she is stainless, beyond all praise.

That which is empty of emptiness, empty of sound, that which is empty of emptiness and has a body empty of sound.
